1→---
     2→version: 1.11.1
     3→last_updated: 2026-01-20
     4→status: Finalized
     5→ai_context: Technical architecture for CipherBox. Contains encryption specs, key hierarchy, auth flows, TEE-based IPNS republishing, and system design. For API details see API_SPECIFICATION.md, for sequences see DATA_FLOWS.md.
     6→---
     7→
     8→# CipherBox - Technical Architecture
     9→
    10→**Document Type:** Technical Specification
    11→**Status:** Finalized
    12→**Last Updated:** January 20, 2026  
    13→
    14→---
    15→
    16→## Table of Contents
    17→
    18→1. [System Overview](#1-system-overview)
    19→2. [Authentication Architecture](#2-authentication-architecture)
    20→3. [Encryption Architecture](#3-encryption-architecture)
    21→4. [Key Management](#4-key-management)
    22→5. [IPFS & IPNS Architecture](#5-ipfs--ipns-architecture)
    23→6. [Tech Stack](#6-tech-stack)
    24→7. [Threat Model](#7-threat-model)
    25→8. [Acceptance Criteria](#8-acceptance-criteria)
    26→9. [TEE-Based IPNS Republishing Architecture](#9-tee-based-ipns-republishing-architecture)
    27→
    28→---
    29→
    30→## Terminology
    31→
    32→| Term | Code/API | Prose | Notes |
    33→|------|----------|-------|-------|
    34→| Root folder encryption key | `rootFolderKey` | root folder key | AES-256 symmetric key |
    35→| User's ECDSA public key | `publicKey` | public key | secp256k1 curve |
    36→| User's ECDSA private key | `privateKey` | private key | Never stored/transmitted |
    37→| IPNS identifier | `ipnsName` | IPNS name | e.g., k51qzi5uqu5dlvj55... |
    38→| IPNS signed data structure | `ipnsRecord` | IPNS record | Contains encrypted metadata |
    39→| Folder encryption key | `folderKey` | folder key | Per-folder AES-256 key |
    40→| File encryption key | `fileKey` | file key | Per-file AES-256 key |
    41→| IPNS signing key | `ipnsPrivateKey` | IPNS private key | Ed25519, stored encrypted |
    42→| TEE public key | `teePublicKey` | TEE public key | Current epoch key for IPNS key encryption |
    43→| TEE epoch | `teeEpoch` | TEE epoch | Key rotation epoch identifier |
    44→| Encrypted IPNS key (for TEE) | `encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` | encrypted IPNS private key | IPNS key encrypted with TEE public key |
    45→
    46→---
    47→
    48→## 1. System Overview
    49→
    50→### 1.1 Architecture Diagram
    51→
    52→```
    53→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    54→│                    End User Devices                         │
    55→├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    56→│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐                 │
    57→│  │   Web Browser    │  │  Desktop App     │                 │
    58→│  │   (React 18)     │  │  (Tauri/Electron)│                 │
    59→│  │  FUSE: No        │  │  FUSE: Yes       │                 │
    60→│  └────────┬─────────┘  └────────┬─────────┘                 │
    61→│           └──────────┬──────────┘                           │
    62→└──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┘
    63→                       │
    64→          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
    65→          │                         │
    66→          ▼                         ▼
    67→   ┌──────────────┐          ┌─────────────────┐
    68→   │  Web3Auth    │          │  CipherBox      │
    69→   │  Network     │          │  Backend        │
    70→   │              │          │  (NestJS)       │
    71→   │ • Auth UI    │          │                 │
    72→   │ • OAuth      │          │ • JWT/SIWE auth │
    73→   │ • Key derive │          │ • Token mgmt    │
    74→   │ • Group conn │          │ • File upload   │
    75→   │              │          │ • Vault mgmt    │
    76→   └──────────────┘          └────────┬────────┘
    77→                                      │
    78→                ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
    79→                │                     │                     │
    80→                ▼                     ▼                     ▼
    81→         ┌────────────┐        ┌──────────┐          ┌─────────┐
    82→         │ PostgreSQL │        │ Pinata   │          │ IPFS    │
    83→         │            │        │ (Pinning)│          │ Network │
    84→         │ • Users    │        │          │          │         │
    85→         │ • Vaults   │        │ Pins     │          │ P2P     │
    86→         │ • Tokens   │        │ encrypted│          │ Storage │
    87→         │ • Audit    │        │ data     │          │         │
    88→         │ • TEE keys │        └──────────┘          └─────────┘
    89→         │ • Republish│               ▲
    90→         │   schedule │               │
    91→         └────────────┘               │
    92→                │                     │
    93→                ▼                     │
    94→         ┌─────────────────┐          │
    95→         │  TEE Provider   │──────────┘
    96→         │  (Phala Cloud)  │   IPNS Republish
    97→         │                 │
    98→         │ • Hardware TEE  │
    99→         │ • Key decrypt   │
   100→         │ • IPNS signing  │
   101→         │ • Key discard   │
   102→         │                 │
   103→         │ Fallback:       │
   104→         │ AWS Nitro       │
   105→         └─────────────────┘
   106→```
   107→
   108→### 1.2 Core Principles
   109→
   110→1. **Zero-Knowledge Server:** Backend never holds plaintext files or unencrypted keys
   111→2. **Client-Side Encryption:** All encryption/decryption happens in browser or desktop app
   112→3. **Deterministic Keys:** Same user + any linked auth method → same ECDSA keypair
   113→4. **Decentralized Storage:** Files stored on IPFS, metadata in IPNS records
   114→5. **User-Held Keys:** Private key exists only in client RAM during session
   115→6. **Signed-Record Relay:** Clients sign IPNS records; backend relays to IPFS/IPNS
   116→
   117→---
   118→
   119→## 2. Authentication Architecture
   120→
   121→### 2.1 Two-Phase Authentication
   122→
   123→CipherBox uses a two-phase authentication approach:
   124→
   125→1. **Phase 1 (Web3Auth):** User authenticates to derive ECDSA keypair
   126→2. **Phase 2 (CipherBox Backend):** User authenticates to obtain access/refresh tokens
   127→
   128→```mermaid
   129→sequenceDiagram
   130→    participant U as User
   131→    participant C as Client
   132→    participant W as Web3Auth
   133→    participant B as CipherBox Backend
   134→    participant DB as PostgreSQL
   135→    
   136→    U->>C: Click "Sign In"
   137→    C->>W: Redirect to login
   138→    U->>W: Complete auth (Google/Email/Wallet)
   139→    W->>W: Derive ECDSA keypair (group connections)
   140→    W->>C: Return keypair + ID token
   141→    C->>B: POST /auth/login {idToken, publicKey}
   142→    B->>B: Verify JWT via JWKS
   143→    B->>DB: Find/create user by publicKey
   144→    B->>C: {accessToken, refreshToken}
   145→    C->>B: GET /my-vault
   146→    B->>C: {encryptedRootFolderKey, rootIpnsName}
   147→    C->>C: Decrypt rootFolderKey with privateKey
   148→```
   149→
   150→### 2.2 Supported Auth Methods (via Web3Auth)
   151→
   152→| Method | Flow | Notes |
   153→|--------|------|-------|
   154→| Email + Password | Web3Auth verifies credentials | Password never sent to CipherBox |
   155→| OAuth (Google/Apple/GitHub) | Standard OAuth via Web3Auth | Token verified by Web3Auth |
   156→| Magic Link | Email link via Web3Auth | Passwordless |
   157→| External Wallet | MetaMask/WalletConnect signature | Trustless, wallet proves identity |
   158→
   159→### 2.3 Web3Auth Group Connections
   160→
   161→All auth methods in the same group derive identical ECDSA keypairs:
   162→
   163→```typescript
   164→const modalConfig = {
   165→  connectors: {
   166→    [WALLET_CONNECTORS.AUTH]: {
   167→      loginMethods: {
   168→        google: {
   169→          authConnectionId: 'w3a-google',
   170→          groupedAuthConnectionId: 'cipherbox-aggregate',  // Group ID
   171→        },
   172→        email_passwordless: {
   173→          authConnectionId: 'w3a-email-passwordless',
   174→          groupedAuthConnectionId: 'cipherbox-aggregate',  // Same group
   175→        },
   176→      },
   177→    },
   178→  },
   179→};
   180→```
   181→
   182→**Key Property:** `same user + any grouped auth method → same keypair → same vault`
   183→
   184→### 2.4 CipherBox Backend Authentication Options
   185→
   186→After Web3Auth key derivation, client authenticates with backend:
   187→
   188→**Option A: Web3Auth ID Token (JWT)**
   189→- Client sends ID token to backend
   190→- Backend verifies via Web3Auth JWKS endpoint
   191→- Simpler flow, relies on Web3Auth token signing
   192→
   193→**Option B: SIWE-like Signature**
   194→- Client requests nonce from backend
   195→- Client signs message with private key
   196→- Backend verifies signature recovers to claimed public key
   197→- More control, doesn't rely on Web3Auth tokens
   198→
   199→### 2.5 Token Architecture
   200→

Now I have a comprehensive understanding. Let me create a detailed summary document with all the findings: Based on my thorough analysis of the CipherBox codebase, here's the complete picture of how MFA status is determined and what the discrepancy you're seeing likely means: ## MFA Status Determination **Location:** `/Users/michael/Code/cipher-box/apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` (lines 34-57) The MFA status is determined entirely by **Web3Auth's MPC Core Kit**: ```typescript const checkMfaStatus = useCallback((): { isMfaEnabled: boolean; totalFactors: number; threshold: number; } => { const details = coreKit.getKeyDetails(); const enabled = details.totalFactors >= 2; // ← MFA enabled when >= 2 factors useMfaStore.getState().setFactorDetails(details.totalFactors, details.threshold); return { isMfaEnabled: enabled, totalFactors: details.totalFactors, threshold: details.threshold, }; }, [coreKit]); ``` ## What Counts as a "Factor" In Web3Auth MPC Core Kit terminology, a **factor** is a TSS (Threshold Secret Sharing) share. The code shows three types of factors: 1. **DEVICE Factor** (`TssShareType.DEVICE`) - Created via `coreKit.createFactor({ shareType: TssShareType.DEVICE, ... })` 2. **RECOVERY Factor** (`TssShareType.RECOVERY`) - The 24-word recovery phrase, created atomically with device factor 3. **HASHED_SHARE** - Internal Web3Auth share (not displayed to user) **`totalFactors` is the count of unique factor public keys** from `details.shareDescriptions` object where each key is a factor's compressed public key hex. ## The Enrollment Flow **Location:** `/Users/michael/Code/cipher-box/apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` (lines 63-113) When a user calls `enableMfa()`: 1. `coreKit.enableMFA({})` is called - **this creates TWO factors automatically**: - A **device factor** (current device's TSS share) - A **recovery factor** (backup recovery phrase share) 2. The recovery phrase is converted to a 24-word mnemonic from the backup factor key 3. Both factors are committed via `coreKit.commitChanges()` 4. Here's the full picture:

## How MFA Status Works

The MFA status comes entirely from **Web3Auth's MPC Core Kit**, not from CipherBox's backend. In `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts:34-57`:

```typescript
const details = coreKit.getKeyDetails();
const enabled = details.totalFactors >= 2;  // MFA = enabled when >= 2 factors
```

Web3Auth uses **Threshold Secret Sharing (TSS)**. The "factors" are TSS shares, and `totalFactors` / `threshold` come from `coreKit.getKeyDetails()`.

## Why You See "2 factors active" Without Enrolling

Web3Auth's MPC Core Kit can have **internal factors** that don't correspond to user-visible device factors or recovery phrases. The key question is what `getKeyDetails().shareDescriptions` actually contains for your account.

The CipherBox UI enumerates factors by parsing `shareDescriptions` and filtering for specific module types (`DeviceShare`, `webDeviceShare`, `seedPhrase`). If the 2 factors are internal Web3Auth types (e.g., `HashedShare` or social login shares), they'd count toward `totalFactors` but **wouldn't show up** in the device list or recovery phrase section.

## The Display Logic

In `SecurityTab.tsx`:
- **MFA badge**: `[ENABLED]` if `totalFactors >= 2`
- **Device list**: Only shows factors with module type `DeviceShare` or `webDeviceShare`
- **Recovery phrase**: Only shows if a `seedPhrase` type factor exists

## What Likely Happened

Your staging account probably has 2 Web3Auth-internal TSS shares (e.g., the social login share + a hashed share), which makes Core Kit report `totalFactors=2`. But since you never ran `enableMfa()` (which creates an explicit device factor + recovery phrase), the enumerable user-facing factors are empty.

Open browser console on staging and run:

```javascript

const details = coreKit.getKeyDetails();
console.log('totalFactors:', details.totalFactors);
console.log('threshold:', details.threshold);
console.log('shareDescriptions:', JSON.stringify(details.shareDescriptions, null, 2));
```

- Each row shows: device name (e.g., "Chrome on macOS"), last active timestamp, status tag
- Current device gets `[CURRENT]` tag in green
- Other authorized devices get `[AUTHORIZED]` tag
- `--revoke` button (red text, `#EF4444`) on non-current devices
- Revoke calls `deleteFactor(factorPubHex)` with confirmation dialog
- Show warning if trying to revoke would leave fewer than 2 factors (the SDK enforces this, but show UX warning proactively)
- If no factors loaded yet, show loading skeleton

**Factor-to-device matching algorithm:** Core Kit factors (from `getKeyDetails().shareDescriptions`) are keyed by factor public key hex. Each value is an array of JSON-encoded description strings. Parse each description to extract:

1. `module` field: identifies factor type ('deviceShare', 'seedPhrase', 'hashedShare', etc.)
2. `additionalMetadata` field: may contain `browserName`, `deviceName`, etc. (set during `createFactor()`)

To match factors to device registry entries:

- For each factor with `module === 'deviceShare'`, check `additionalMetadata` for a `deviceId` field (we set this in Plan 04 during `createFactor()`)
- If `additionalMetadata.deviceId` exists, match against `useDeviceRegistryStore` entries by deviceId to get the friendly name and last active time
- If no `deviceId` in metadata (factors created before this phase), show "Unknown device" with the factor's creation date
- For the CURRENT device: use `useMfa().getCurrentFactorKey()` to get the current factor's public key, compare against the factor list to tag one row as `[CURRENT]`
- For `module === 'seedPhrase'` factors: do NOT show in the device list (these are recovery phrases, shown in RecoveryPhraseSection)
- For `module === 'hashedShare'` factors: do NOT show (this is the cloud custodial key, which is deleted by enableMFA)

**RecoveryPhraseSection** (`RecoveryPhraseSection.tsx`):
Uses `useMfa()` hook for `regenerateRecoveryPhrase()` and `getFactors()`.

Shows:

- Recovery phrase status: "Active" with green dot (if recovery factor exists in factors list, detected by module='seedPhrase')
- `--regenerate` button
- When clicked: confirmation warning ("This will invalidate your current recovery phrase. Are you sure?")
- On confirm: calls `regenerateRecoveryPhrase()`, shows the new RecoveryPhraseGrid in a modal/inline expansion
- Same `[x]` checkbox confirmation required for the new phrase
- Red warning about invalidating old phrase

**SecurityTab** (`SecurityTab.tsx`):
Uses `useMfa()` hook for `checkMfaStatus()`.

Layout:

- MFA status badge at top: green dot + `[ENABLED]` or red dot + `[DISABLED]` (matching Pencil mockup)

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the Web3Auth MPC Core Kit's `enableMFA` method and the hashed share behavior:

The hashed cloud factor is deleted when the user enables the MFA. This is consistent across the documentation, as the same information appears in multiple sources.

Additionally, the usage examples confirm this behavior: "MFA enabled, device factor stored in local store, deleted hashed cloud key, your backup factor key:" - this is the console output shown when `enableMFA()` is called.

Regarding the factor count, the threshold is the minimum number of shares required to generate a final signature for the TSS Account. By default, the Web3Auth Network requires 3 out of 5 shares (3/5) to generate a signature. This means that out of the 5 shares distributed across different nodes, any 3 shares can be combined to create the final signature.

The search results show that when `enableMFA()` is invoked, the hashed share (which is part of the initial 2/2 factor setup) is **deleted** and replaced with a device factor and backup factor, effectively changing the account's factor structure from a 2/2 flow to a more secure non-custodial setup.

content.text:
That confirms it. Here's the full picture:

## The `hashedShare` role

The `hashedShare` is a **cloud custodial key** — it's Web3Auth's "training wheels" factor that exists on every fresh account. It makes the initial 2/2 setup seamless (user logs in with JWT, the hashedShare is automatically retrieved from Web3Auth's network, both shares combine to sign).

## What `enableMFA()` does

When `enableMFA()` is called, it:
1. **Deletes the `hashedShare`** (removes the cloud custodial key)
2. **Creates a device factor** (stored locally)
3. **Creates a backup/recovery factor** (returned as the mnemonic)

So the account goes from semi-custodial (Web3Auth can reconstruct your key via the hashedShare) to fully non-custodial (only your devices + recovery phrase can reconstruct it).

## Your staging account state

- `totalFactors: 2` — the JWT verifier share + the `hashedShare`
- This is the **default pre-MFA state** for every account
- `enableMFA()` was never called, so the hashedShare was never deleted

## On your `> 2` fix suggestion

Your plan doc at `.planning/phases/12.4-mfa-cross-device/12.4-03-PLAN.md:165` says it correctly: the hashedShare "is deleted by enableMFA". After `enableMFA()`, the hashedShare is gone and replaced by device + recovery factors, so `totalFactors` would be at least 3 (JWT share + device + recovery).

So yes — **`totalFactors > 2` should work** and is much simpler than parsing `shareDescriptions`. The baseline is always 2 (JWT + hashedShare), and `enableMFA()` deletes one and adds two, pushing it to 3+.

Sources:
- [Web3Auth MPC Core Kit JS SDK](https://web3auth.io/docs/sdk/mpc-core-kit/mpc-core-kit-js)
- [MPC Core Kit Examples](https://github.com/Web3Auth/mpc-core-kit-examples/blob/main/mpc-core-kit-web/quick-starts/mpc-core-kit-nextjs-quick-start/app/page.tsx)
- [Web3Auth MPC Architecture](https://web3auth.io/docs/infrastructure/mpc-architecture)

content.text:
<objective>
Execute small, ad-hoc tasks with GSD guarantees (atomic commits, STATE.md tracking) while skipping optional agents (research, plan-checker, verifier).

Quick mode is the same system with a shorter path:

- Spawns gsd-planner (quick mode) + gsd-executor(s)
- Skips gsd-phase-researcher, gsd-plan-checker, gsd-verifier
- Quick tasks live in `.planning/quick/` separate from planned phases
- Updates STATE.md "Quick Tasks Completed" table (NOT ROADMAP.md)

**For UI tasks:**

- Detects UI-related task descriptions
- Offers to generate/use Pencil designs before planning
- Optionally verifies against design with Playwright MCP after execution

Use when: You know exactly what to do and the task is small enough to not need research or verification.
</objective>

<execution_context>
Orchestration is inline - no separate workflow file. Quick mode is deliberately simpler than full GSD.
</execution_context>

<context>
@.planning/STATE.md
</context>

<process>
### Step 1: Pre-flight validation

Check that an active GSD project exists:

```bash
if [ ! -f .planning/ROADMAP.md ]; then
  echo "Quick mode requires an active project with ROADMAP.md."
  echo "Run /gsd:new-project first."
  exit 1
fi
```

If validation fails, stop immediately with the error message.

Quick tasks can run mid-phase - validation only checks ROADMAP.md exists, not phase status.

---

### Step 2: Get task description

Prompt user interactively for the task description:

```text
AskUserQuestion(
  header: "Quick Task",
  question: "What do you want to do?",
  followUp: null
)
```

Store response as `$DESCRIPTION`.

If empty, re-prompt: "Please provide a task description."

Generate slug from description:

```bash
slug=$(echo "$DESCRIPTION" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]/-/g' | sed 's/--*/-/g' | sed 's/^-//;s/-$//' | cut -c1-40)
```

**Scan learnings** for relevant context:

```bash
ls .learnings/*.md 2>/dev/null | grep -v README
```

If entries exist, quickly scan titles and read any that relate to the task description. Extract gotchas, patterns, and key files that may be relevant. This prevents repeating past mistakes. Skip if no `.learnings/` directory exists.

---

### Step 2b: Detect UI task and offer design workflow

Check if the task description involves UI work:

```bash
# Check for UI keywords in description
# Note: This heuristic may produce false positives for tasks that mention UI terms
# in non-UI contexts (e.g., "update button text in config"). The user can always
# select "Skip design - just implement" if the detection is incorrect.
if echo "$DESCRIPTION" | grep -iqE "ui|ux|style|restyle|design|layout|component|page|view|screen|display|button|form|modal|dialog|popover|tooltip|toast|dropdown|sidebar|header|footer|nav|menu|card|list|table|grid|icon|badge|avatar|breadcrumb|tab|color|font|typography|spacing|padding|margin|responsive|mobile|css|visual|appearance|interface|frontend|dashboard|browser|drag|drop|dnd|hover|focus|animation|transition|overlay|scroll|carousel|interaction|gesture|click|swipe|resize|collapse|expand|accordion|input|checkbox|radio|select|slider|toggle|switch|picker|upload|panel|drawer|toolbar|statusbar|banner|alert|notification|snackbar|thumbnail|preview|placeholder|skeleton|spinner|progress|loading"; then
  IS_UI_TASK=true
else
  IS_UI_TASK=false
fi
```

**If UI task detected:**

1. Check for existing Pencil design file:

```bash
DESIGN_FILE=$(ls designs/*.pen 2>/dev/null | head -1)
if [ -z "$DESIGN_FILE" ]; then
  echo "No design file found in designs/. Will proceed without design reference."
fi
```

2. Offer design workflow:

```text
AskUserQuestion(
  header: "UI Task Detected",
  question: "This looks like a UI task. How would you like to proceed?",
  options: [
    "Use existing Pencil design" (if design file exists),
    "Generate new design mockup first",
    "Skip design - just implement"
  ]
)
```

3. **If "Use existing design":**
   - Load design tokens from existing `.pen` file
   - Ask which frame/component to reference
   - Store design reference for planner context

4. **If "Generate new mockup":**

   First, load existing design context for consistency:

   ```typescript
   // Load existing design system
   const existingDesign = await mcp__pencil__read_design({ path: DESIGN_FILE });
   const tokens = await mcp__pencil__get_design_tokens({
     file: DESIGN_FILE,
     extract: ['colors', 'typography', 'spacing', 'effects', 'borders'],
   });
   ```

   Then, translate user's task description to design parameters:

   ```typescript
   // Parse task description for design intent
   const taskIntent = {
     description: DESCRIPTION, // e.g., "Add a delete confirmation modal"
     componentType: inferComponentType(DESCRIPTION), // e.g., "modal"
     action: inferAction(DESCRIPTION), // e.g., "delete" → destructive styling
   };

   // Map to design parameters using existing tokens
   const designParams = {
     colors: tokens.colors,
     typography: tokens.typography,
     // Adjust for context (e.g., destructive action = error color)
     accentColor: taskIntent.action === 'delete' ? '#EF4444' : tokens.colors.primary,
   };
   ```

   Create mockup with full context:

   ```typescript
   await mcp__pencil__create_design({
     type: 'frame',
     name: `Quick: ${slug}`,
     width: 800,
     height: 600,
     fill: tokens.colors.background,

     // Pass context for consistency
     designContext: {
       tokens: tokens,
       taskIntent: taskIntent,
       referenceFrames: existingDesign.frames.map((f) => f.name),
       consistencyRules: [
         'Use ONLY colors from existing palette',
         'Match existing component patterns',
         'Follow established spacing scale',
       ],
     },

     children: [
       /* generated based on componentType */
     ],
   });
   ```

   - Present to user for approval with design rationale
   - Store approved design reference

5. **If "Skip design":**
   - Proceed without design reference
   - Note: Verification against design will be skipped

Store result as `$DESIGN_CONTEXT` for planner.

---

### Step 3: Calculate next quick task number

Ensure `.planning/quick/` directory exists and find the next sequential number:

```bash
# Ensure .planning/quick/ exists
mkdir -p .planning/quick

# Find highest existing number and increment
last=$(ls -1d .planning/quick/[0-9][0-9][0-9]-* 2>/dev/null | sort -r | head -1 | xargs -I{} basename {} | grep -oE '^[0-9]+')

if [ -z "$last" ]; then
  next_num="001"
else
  next_num=$(printf "%03d" $((10#$last + 1)))
fi
```

---

### Step 4: Create quick task directory

Create the directory for this quick task:

```bash
QUICK_DIR=".planning/quick/${next_num}-${slug}"
mkdir -p "$QUICK_DIR"
```

Report to user:

```text
Creating quick task ${next_num}: ${DESCRIPTION}
Directory: ${QUICK_DIR}
```

Store `$QUICK_DIR` for use in orchestration.

---

### Step 5: Spawn planner (quick mode)

Spawn gsd-planner with quick mode context:

```text
Task(
  prompt="
<planning_context>

**Mode:** quick
**Directory:** ${QUICK_DIR}
**Description:** ${DESCRIPTION}

**Project State:**
@.planning/STATE.md

${DESIGN_CONTEXT ? `
**Design Reference (UI Task):**
- Design file: ${DESIGN_FILE}
- Frame: ${DESIGN_FRAME}
- Design tokens: Use colors, typography, spacing from existing design

Implementation must match Pencil design specifications exactly.
Verification will compare against design frame.
` : ''}

</planning_context>

<constraints>
- Create a SINGLE plan with 1-3 focused tasks
- Quick tasks should be atomic and self-contained
- No research phase, no checker phase
- Target ~30% context usage (simple, focused)
${IS_UI_TASK ? '- Include CSS values from design specs in task descriptions' : ''}
${IS_UI_TASK ? '- Add verification step to check implementation matches design' : ''}
</constraints>

<output>
Write plan to: ${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-PLAN.md
Return: ## PLANNING COMPLETE with plan path
</output>
",
  subagent_type="gsd-planner",
  description="Quick plan: ${DESCRIPTION}"
)
```

After planner returns:

1. Verify plan exists at `${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-PLAN.md`
2. Extract plan count (typically 1 for quick tasks)
3. Report: "Plan created: ${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-PLAN.md"

If plan not found, error: "Planner failed to create ${next_num}-PLAN.md"

---

### Step 6: Spawn executor

Spawn gsd-executor with plan reference:

```text
Task(
  prompt="
Execute quick task ${next_num}.

Plan: @${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-PLAN.md
Project state: @.planning/STATE.md

<constraints>
- Execute all tasks in the plan
- Commit each task atomically
- Create summary at: ${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-SUMMARY.md
- Do NOT update ROADMAP.md (quick tasks are separate from planned phases)
</constraints>
",
  subagent_type="gsd-executor",
  description="Execute: ${DESCRIPTION}"
)
```

After executor returns:

1. Verify summary exists at `${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-SUMMARY.md`
2. Extract commit hash from executor output
3. Report completion status

If summary not found, error: "Executor failed to create ${next_num}-SUMMARY.md"

Note: For quick tasks producing multiple plans (rare), spawn executors in parallel waves per execute-phase patterns.

---

### Step 6b: Quick UI verification (for UI tasks only)

If `IS_UI_TASK=true` and `DESIGN_CONTEXT` exists, offer quick verification:

```text
AskUserQuestion(
  header: "UI Verification",
  question: "Task complete. Would you like me to verify the UI matches the design?",
  options: ["Yes, verify against design", "Skip verification"]
)
```

**If "Yes, verify":**

1. **Use Playwright MCP to verify (if available):**

```typescript
// Navigate to the app
await mcp__playwright__navigate({ url: 'http://localhost:5173' });

// Capture screenshot
await mcp__playwright__screenshot({
  selector: '${COMPONENT_SELECTOR}',
  name: 'quick-${next_num}-result',
});

// Verify computed styles match design
const styles = await mcp__playwright__evaluate({
  script: `
    const el = document.querySelector('${COMPONENT_SELECTOR}');
    const s = getComputedStyle(el);
    return {
      backgroundColor: s.backgroundColor,
      color: s.color,
      fontFamily: s.fontFamily,
      padding: s.padding
    };
  `,
});
```

2. **Compare against design specs:**

```typescript
// Load expected values from design
const designSpecs = await mcp__pencil__get_frame({ frameId: DESIGN_FRAME });

// Compare with tolerance for color format differences
// RGB values are considered matching if they represent the same color:
// - "#000000" matches "rgb(0, 0, 0)"
// - "#00D084" matches "rgb(0, 208, 132)"
// Spacing values must match exactly (no tolerance for pixel differences)
const discrepancies = compareStyles(styles, designSpecs, {
  colorTolerance: 'format-only', // Allow rgb/hex format differences
  spacingTolerance: 0, // Exact pixel match required
});
```

3. **Report results:**

```markdown
## Quick Verification Results

**Component:** ${COMPONENT_SELECTOR}
**Design frame:** ${DESIGN_FRAME}

| Property   | Design    | Implemented    | Status |
| ---------- | --------- | -------------- | ------ |
| background | #000000   | rgb(0,0,0)     | ✓      |
| color      | #00D084   | rgb(0,208,132) | ✓      |
| padding    | 12px 24px | 12px 24px      | ✓      |

**Result:** [All specs match / X discrepancies found]
```

4. **If discrepancies found:**

```text
AskUserQuestion(
  header: "Discrepancies Found",
  question: "Found ${count} discrepancies. What would you like to do?",
  options: ["Fix now", "Accept as-is", "View details"]
)
```

If "Fix now" → Re-run executor with fix instructions
If "Accept as-is" → Continue to STATE.md update
If "View details" → Show full discrepancy report

**If Playwright MCP not available:**

Document for manual verification:

```markdown
## Manual Verification Required

Playwright MCP not available. Please verify manually:

1. Open http://localhost:5173
2. Check ${COMPONENT_SELECTOR}
3. Compare against design frame: ${DESIGN_FRAME}

Expected:

- Background: ${expected_bg}
- Color: ${expected_color}
- Padding: ${expected_padding}
```

---

### Step 6c: Design sync check (UI tasks only)

If `IS_UI_TASK=true` and a `.pen` file exists, offer a lightweight design sync:

```bash
DESIGN_FILE=$(ls designs/*.pen 2>/dev/null | head -1)
```

**Only runs if both conditions are true:**

- `IS_UI_TASK=true`
- `DESIGN_FILE` is non-empty

```bash
# Get changed CSS/TSX files on this branch
CHANGED_UI=$(git diff --name-only main...HEAD -- '*.css' '*.tsx' 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^$')
```

If UI files changed, offer sync check:

```text
AskUserQuestion(
  header: "Design Sync",
  question: "UI files changed on this branch. Check if design needs updating?",
  options: [
    { label: "Yes, sync design", description: "Run lightweight design sync (defaults to updating design to match code)" },
    { label: "Skip", description: "Continue without checking design" }
  ],
  multiSelect: false
)
```

**If "Yes, sync design":**

Run a lightweight version of `/design:sync` inline:

1. Get changed CSS/TSX files (already computed above)
2. Map to design frames using `designs/DESIGN.md` component hierarchy
3. For mapped files: extract CSS values, compare against Pencil frames via `mcp__pencil__batch_get`
4. Default direction: **update design to match code** (code was just written)
5. Apply `mcp__pencil__batch_design` updates for any mismatches
6. Take screenshot to verify
7. Report changes and remind user to save Pencil file

**If "Skip":** Continue to Step 7.

**Non-blocking:** This step never prevents task completion. If Pencil MCP is unavailable or errors occur, log a note and continue.

---

### Step 7: Update STATE.md

Update STATE.md with quick task completion record.

**7a. Check if "Quick Tasks Completed" section exists:**

Read STATE.md and check for `### Quick Tasks Completed` section.

**7b. If section doesn't exist, create it:**

Insert after `### Blockers/Concerns` section:

```markdown
### Quick Tasks Completed

| #   | Description | Date | Commit | Directory |
| --- | ----------- | ---- | ------ | --------- |
```

**7c. Append new row to table:**

```markdown
| ${next_num} | ${DESCRIPTION} | $(date +%Y-%m-%d) | ${commit_hash} | [${next_num}-${slug}](./quick/${next_num}-${slug}/) |
```

**7d. Update "Last activity" line:**

Find and update the line:

```text
Last activity: $(date +%Y-%m-%d) - Completed quick task ${next_num}: ${DESCRIPTION}
```

Use Edit tool to make these changes atomically

---

### Step 8: Final commit and completion

Stage and commit quick task artifacts:

```bash
# Stage quick task artifacts
git add ${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-PLAN.md
git add ${QUICK_DIR}/${next_num}-SUMMARY.md
git add .planning/STATE.md

# For UI tasks: add design file if modified
if [ "$IS_UI_TASK" = true ]; then
  git diff --quiet designs/*.pen 2>/dev/null || git add designs/*.pen
fi

# Commit with quick task format
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
docs(quick-${next_num}): ${DESCRIPTION}

Quick task completed.
${IS_UI_TASK:+- Design mockups added to .pen file}

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"
```

Get final commit hash:

```bash
commit_hash=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
```

**Capture learnings** (skip if trivial):

If the quick task involved non-obvious discoveries, gotchas, or useful patterns, create a learnings entry at `.learnings/YYYY-MM-DD-brief-description.md`:

```markdown
# [Brief Title]

**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD

## Original Prompt

> [User's original task description]

## What I Learned
```

If created, commit it:

```bash
git commit -m "docs(learnings): quick-${next_num} - {brief description}"
```

Display completion output:

```text
GSD > QUICK TASK COMPLETE

Quick Task ${next_num}: ${DESCRIPTION}

---

Ready for next task: /gsd:quick
```

# Phase 12.4 MFA + Cross-Device Approval - Learnings

**Date:** 2026-02-15

## Original Prompt

> Users can enroll in MFA with device shares and recovery phrases, and approve new devices from existing authenticated devices

## What I Learned

- Core Kit `enableMFA()` returns a BN (big number) not a string — need `@tkey/common-types` and `bn.js` as direct deps in pnpm strict mode since transitive deps aren't hoisted
- `loginWithCoreKit` returning a typed union ('logged_in' | 'required_share') is cleaner than try/catch for flow branching — callers can branch without error handling
- Placeholder publicKey pattern for temporary backend auth in REQUIRED_SHARE state works well — `pending-core-kit-{userId}` allows API access before TSS key is available
- Noble secp256k1 v3 API uses `keygen()` returning `{ secretKey, publicKey }` instead of v2's `utils.randomPrivateKey()` — API surface changed between major versions
- Auto-expire on read (filtering out expired requests during getStatus/getPending) is simpler and more reliable than background cron for short TTL (5 minutes)
- Parallel agents committing to the same branch can cause lint-staged stash conflicts — files from one agent's stash get pulled into another agent's commit. Non-harmful but messy.

## What Would Have Helped

- Knowing Core Kit's `getKeyDetails()` return shape upfront (threshold, totalFactors, shareDescriptions map)
- Clear documentation on how `shareDescriptions` stores device metadata (JSON stringified in a Map keyed by factor public key)
- Understanding that `keyType` in factor info is a Core Kit internal, not directly useful for device vs recovery distinction

## Key Files

- `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` — Central MFA operations hook (276 lines)
- `apps/web/src/hooks/useDeviceApproval.ts` — Full approval lifecycle with ECIES key exchange (380 lines)
- `apps/web/src/lib/web3auth/hooks.ts` — Core Kit login with REQUIRED_SHARE handling
- `apps/api/src/device-approval/` — Bulletin board REST API (entity, service, controller, module, DTOs)
- `apps/web/src/components/mfa/` — All MFA UI components (wizard, security tab, devices, approval modal, waiting screen, recovery)

- This gives every fresh account `totalFactors: 2` and `threshold: 2` 
- Current code at `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts:46` checks `details.totalFactors >= 2` which is ALWAYS true
- After `enableMFA()`, the hashedShare is deleted and replaced by device + recovery factors, so totalFactors becomes 3+
- Fix: change `>= 2` to `> 2`

**Key files:**
- `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` — line 46: `const enabled = details.totalFactors >= 2;`

- `apps/web/src/components/mfa/SecurityTab.tsx` — displays MFA badge based on store state

- Core Kit `enableMFA()` returns a BN (big number)
- `getKeyDetails()` returns `{ threshold, totalFactors, shareDescriptions }` map

patterns-established: []

# Quick Task 022: Fix MFA Status Detection False Positive Summary

**Changed MFA detection threshold from `>= 2` to `> 2` to account for 2 default Core Kit factors (JWT verifier + hashedShare)**

## Performance

- **Duration:** 2 min
- **Started:** 2026-02-26T18:56:02Z
- **Completed:** 2026-02-26T18:57:45Z
- **Tasks:** 1
- **Files modified:** 1

## Accomplishments
- Fixed false-positive MFA status: fresh accounts no longer show [ENABLED]
- Updated JSDoc comment explaining the 2-default-factor reasoning
- SecurityTab, MfaEnrollmentWizard, and DeviceApprovalModal all consume `isMfaEnabled` from the store -- no downstream changes needed

## Task Commits

Each task was committed atomically:

1. **Task 1: Fix MFA status threshold check and update comment** - `ff850e0e7` (fix)

## Files Created/Modified
- `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` - Changed `details.totalFactors >= 2` to `details.totalFactors > 2` and updated JSDoc comment

## Decisions Made
- Threshold `> 2` is correct because every Web3Auth MPC Core Kit account starts with exactly 2 factors: the JWT verifier share and the hashedShare (cloud custodial key). After `enableMFA()`, the hashedShare is deleted and replaced by device + recovery factors, pushing totalFactors to 3+.

## Deviations from Plan

None - plan executed exactly as written.

## Issues Encountered

None

## User Setup Required

None - no external service configuration required.

## Next Phase Readiness
- MFA status detection is now accurate
- No follow-up work needed

<objective>
Fix false-positive MFA status detection in useMfa.ts.

Purpose: Every Web3Auth MPC Core Kit account starts with 2 factors by default (JWT verifier share + hashedShare cloud custodial key). The current check `details.totalFactors >= 2` is ALWAYS true, so MFA falsely shows as [ENABLED] for every user. After `enableMFA()` is called, the hashedShare is deleted and replaced by device + recovery factors, pushing totalFactors to 3+. The fix is changing `>= 2` to `> 2`.

Output: Corrected `useMfa.ts` where `checkMfaStatus` correctly detects MFA as disabled for fresh accounts and enabled only after enrollment.
</objective>

message.content:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Analysis:
Let me chronologically analyze the conversation:

1. **Initial Request**: User wants to understand the MFA setup - their account on staging never went through MFA enrollment, but the security page shows MFA as "[ENABLED]" with "2 factors active, 2/2 threshold". They provided their public key and a screenshot of the security page.

2. **My Initial Research**: I spawned an Explore agent to investigate the MFA code. Found key files:
   - `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` - Central MFA hook
   - `apps/web/src/stores/mfa.store.ts` - Zustand store
   - `apps/web/src/components/mfa/SecurityTab.tsx` - UI component
   - `apps/web/src/components/mfa/AuthorizedDevices.tsx` - Device list
   - `apps/web/src/components/mfa/RecoveryPhraseSection.tsx` - Recovery phrase UI

3. **Initial Explanation**: I explained that MFA status comes from Web3Auth's MPC Core Kit via `coreKit.getKeyDetails()`, and `totalFactors >= 2` marks MFA as enabled. I initially (incorrectly) attributed the 2 factors to "social login share + hashedShare".

4. **Playwright Session**: User asked to start a Playwright session pointed at staging. I navigated to https://app-staging.cipherbox.cc, user logged in, then I navigated to Settings > Security tab and confirmed the issue visually.

5. **Console Investigation**: I used Playwright's evaluate to dig into Core Kit's state. After several attempts (finding React fiber root key was `__reactContainer` not `__reactFiber`), I successfully extracted the key details:
   ```json
   {
     "totalFactors": 2,
     "threshold": 2,
     "requiredFactors": 0,
     "shareDescriptions": {
       "024b05fc...": [
         "{\"module\":\"hashedShare\",\"dateAdded\":1771472255283,\"tssShareIndex\":2}"
       ]
     }
   }
   ```

6. **User Correction**: I initially said "social login share" was one of the factors. User corrected me: "there is no social login share - all initial auth with w3auth is via a cipherbox jwt configured as a custom provider with w3auth". I acknowledged the correction and updated my understanding.

7. **User's Key Questions**: User asked:
   - "What role does the hashedShare even play?"
   - "What is your assessment of this just being created by Core Kit based on?"
   - "Would an easier fix not just be `const enabled = details.totalFactors > 2`?"

8. **Research on hashedShare**: I searched Web3Auth docs (many 404s), found key info:
   - `.planning/phases/12.4-mfa-cross-device/12.4-03-PLAN.md:165` says: "For `module === 'hashedShare'` factors: do NOT show (this is the cloud custodial key, which is deleted by enableMFA)"
   - Web search confirmed: "MFA enabled, device factor stored in local store, deleted hashed cloud key"
   - The hashedShare is a cloud custodial key, deleted when enableMFA() is called

9. **Fix Confirmation**: Confirmed that `totalFactors > 2` is the correct simple fix because:
   - Baseline: 2 factors (JWT verifier + hashedShare)
   - After enableMFA(): hashedShare deleted, device + recovery added = 3+ factors

10. **GSD Quick Task Execution**: User asked to use `/gsd:quick` to implement the fix. I:
    - Created branch `fix/mfa-status-false-positive` from latest main
    - Created quick task directory `.planning/quick/022-fix-mfa-status-detection-false-positive/`
    - Spawned gsd-planner (created 022-PLAN.md)
    - Spawned gsd-executor (created fix + 022-SUMMARY.md)
    - Fixed markdown lint error (fenced code blocks needed language specifiers)
    - Final commits: ff850e0 (code fix), 580e606 (docs/summary), e36a788 (plan)

Key files read:
- `apps/web/src/hooks/useMfa.ts` - The main fix location
- `apps/web/src/lib/web3auth/core-kit-provider.tsx` - CoreKit React context
- `apps/web/src/lib/web3auth/core-kit.ts` - CoreKit singleton
- `apps/web/src/stores/mfa.store.ts` - Zustand MFA store
- `apps/web/src/components/mfa/SecurityTab.tsx` - Security tab UI
- `apps/web/src/components/mfa/AuthorizedDevices.tsx` - Device list component
- `apps/web/src/components/mfa/RecoveryPhraseSection.tsx` - Recovery phrase component
- `.planning/phases/12.4-mfa-cross-device/12.4-03-PLAN.md` - Planning doc with hashedShare info
- `.learnings/2026-02-15-phase-12.4-mfa-cross-device.md` - MFA learnings

The fix was a single character change: `>=` to `>` on line 46 of useMfa.ts, plus a comment update.

Errors encountered:
1. Git index.lock file existed - removed it
2. Markdown lint failed on plan file (fenced code blocks without language) - fixed by adding `text` language specifier
3. React fiber key was `__reactContainer` not `__reactFiber` - adjusted query

User messages to capture:
1. Initial question about MFA setup
2. "ok logged in"

content.thinking:
The user is asking about the security implications of the "semi-custodial" state I mentioned earlier - specifically how Web3Auth could theoretically reconstruct the user's key using the hashedShare.

Let me think about the MPC Core Kit architecture:

1. **MPC Core Kit uses Threshold Secret Sharing (TSS)** - the private key is split into shares distributed across multiple parties
2. **In the default (pre-MFA) state**, there are 2 factors with threshold 2:
   - Factor 1: JWT verifier share (held by Web3Auth's distributed key infrastructure/nodes)
   - Factor 2: hashedShare (cloud custodial key, also stored on Web3Auth's infrastructure)


3. **The critical distinction**: The verifier share is distributed across Web3Auth's node network through their distributed key generation, while the hashedShare sits on their metadata server - but the key itself never gets reconstructed in full on any single node since signing happens distributedly through TSS.

So the real risk isn't Web3Auth casually reconstructing your key, but rather a coordinated attack requiring collusion across multiple nodes plus access to the metadata storage.

Once MFA is enabled, the threat model shifts dramatically—Web3Auth loses access to the hashedShare entirely, and even if all their nodes collude, they're left with just the verifier share, which is useless without either your device share or recovery phrase. The user's concern about collusion is valid, but it's a much higher bar than a single compromised server.

content.text:
Good question. The MPC Core Kit architecture makes it more nuanced than a simple "Web3Auth has your key":

**How the verifier share works:**

The JWT verifier share isn't held by a single Web3Auth server — it's distributed across their node network using Distributed Key Generation (DKG). No single node holds the full verifier share. So yes, reconstructing that piece would require collusion among a threshold of Web3Auth nodes.

**The hashedShare piece:**

The hashedShare is stored on Web3Auth's metadata server (their cloud infrastructure). It's a separate system from the DKG nodes.

**Semi-custodial means:**

In the 2/2 pre-MFA state, both factors are ultimately within Web3Auth's infrastructure:
1. Verifier share → distributed across their node network (needs node collusion)
2. hashedShare → on their metadata server

So reconstruction would require **both**: enough DKG nodes colluding to reconstruct the verifier share **and** access to the metadata server for the hashedShare. The MPC architecture makes this harder than a single-server custodial model, but since Web3Auth operates both systems, the trust boundary is still within one organization.

**After enableMFA():**

The hashedShare is deleted and replaced with a device share (local to user's device) + recovery phrase (user-controlled). Now even if all Web3Auth nodes collude, they only have 1 of the 2 required factors. The second factor is outside their infrastructure entirely.

That's the real security upgrade — it moves the trust boundary from "trust Web3Auth's infrastructure" to "trust that your device + Web3Auth nodes won't both be compromised."

    40→| File encryption key | `fileKey` | file key | Per-file AES-256 key |
    41→| IPNS signing key | `ipnsPrivateKey` | IPNS private key | Ed25519, stored encrypted |
    42→| TEE public key | `teePublicKey` | TEE public key | Current epoch key for IPNS key encryption |
    43→| TEE epoch | `teeEpoch` | TEE epoch | Key rotation epoch identifier |
    44→| Encrypted IPNS key (for TEE) | `encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` | encrypted IPNS private key | IPNS key encrypted with TEE public key |

   108→### 1.2 Core Principles
   109→
   110→1. **Zero-Knowledge Server:** Backend never holds plaintext files or unencrypted keys
   111→2. **Client-Side Encryption:** All encryption/decryption happens in browser or desktop app
   112→3. **Deterministic Keys:** Same user + any linked auth method → same ECDSA keypair
   113→4. **Decentralized Storage:** Files stored on IPFS, metadata in IPNS records
   114→5. **User-Held Keys:** Private key exists only in client RAM during session
   115→6. **Signed-Record Relay:** Clients sign IPNS records; backend relays to IPFS/IPNS

   119→## 2. Authentication Architecture
   120→
   121→### 2.1 Two-Phase Authentication
   122→
   123→CipherBox uses a two-phase authentication approach:
   124→
   125→1. **Phase 1 (Web3Auth):** User authenticates to derive ECDSA keypair
   126→2. **Phase 2 (CipherBox Backend):** User authenticates to obtain access/refresh tokens
   127→
   128→```mermaid
   129→sequenceDiagram
   130→    participant U as User
   131→    participant C as Client
   132→    participant W as Web3Auth
   133→    participant B as CipherBox Backend
   134→    participant DB as PostgreSQL
   135→    
   136→    U->>C: Click "Sign In"
   137→    C->>W: Redirect to login
   138→    U->>W: Complete auth (Google/Email/Wallet)
   139→    W->>W: Derive ECDSA keypair (group connections)
   140→    W->>C: Return keypair + ID token
   141→    C->>B: POST /auth/login {idToken, publicKey}
   142→    B->>B: Verify JWT via JWKS
   143→    B->>DB: Find/create user by publicKey
   144→    B->>C: {accessToken, refreshToken}
   145→    C->>B: GET /my-vault
   146→    B->>C: {encryptedRootFolderKey, rootIpnsName}
   147→    C->>C: Decrypt rootFolderKey with privateKey
   148→```
   149→
   150→### 2.2 Supported Auth Methods (via Web3Auth)
   151→
   152→| Method | Flow | Notes |
   153→|--------|------|-------|
   154→| Email + Password | Web3Auth verifies credentials | Password never sent to CipherBox |
   155→| OAuth (Google/Apple/GitHub) | Standard OAuth via Web3Auth | Token verified by Web3Auth |
   156→| Magic Link | Email link via Web3Auth | Passwordless |
   157→| External Wallet | MetaMask/WalletConnect signature | Trustless, wallet proves identity |
   158→
   159→### 2.3 Web3Auth Group Connections
   160→
   161→All auth methods in the same group derive identical ECDSA keypairs:
   162→
   163→```typescript
   164→const modalConfig = {
   165→  connectors: {
   166→    [WALLET_CONNECTORS.AUTH]: {
   167→      loginMethods: {
   168→        google: {
   169→          authConnectionId: 'w3a-google',
   170→          groupedAuthConnectionId: 'cipherbox-aggregate',  // Group ID
   171→        },
   172→        email_passwordless: {
   173→          authConnectionId: 'w3a-email-passwordless',
   174→          groupedAuthConnectionId: 'cipherbox-aggregate',  // Same group
   175→        },
   176→      },
   177→    },
   178→  },
   179→};
   180→```
   181→
   182→**Key Property:** `same user + any grouped auth method → same keypair → same vault`
   183→
   184→### 2.4 CipherBox Backend Authentication Options
   185→
   186→After Web3Auth key derivation, client authenticates with backend:
   187→
   188→**Option A: Web3Auth ID Token (JWT)**
   189→- Client sends ID token to backend
   190→- Backend verifies via Web3Auth JWKS endpoint
   191→- Simpler flow, relies on Web3Auth token signing
   192→
   193→**Option B: SIWE-like Signature**
   194→- Client requests nonce from backend
   195→- Client signs message with private key
   196→- Backend verifies signature recovers to claimed public key
   197→- More control, doesn't rely on Web3Auth tokens
   198→
   199→### 2.5 Token Architecture
   200→
   201→| Token | Issuer | Expiry | Storage | Purpose |
   202→|-------|--------|--------|---------|---------|
   203→| Web3Auth ID Token | Web3Auth | 1 hour | Memory | Authenticate with CipherBox backend |
   204→| Access Token | CipherBox | 15 min | Memory only | API authorization |
   205→| Refresh Token | CipherBox | 7 days | HTTP-only cookie or encrypted storage | Obtain new access tokens |
   206→
   207→### 2.6 Web3Auth Key Export (Recovery Path)
   208→
   209→Users can export their Web3Auth private key for disaster recovery:
   210→
   211→```
   212→Normal flow: User → Web3Auth → keypair → vault access
   213→
   214→Recovery flow (Web3Auth unavailable):
   215→1. User has previously exported Web3Auth private key
   216→2. User imports key directly into CipherBox recovery tool
   217→3. Tool derives publicKey from privateKey
   218→4. Tool decrypts vault export using privateKey
   219→5. User has full vault access without Web3Auth
   220→
   221→Note: Direct key import bypasses Web3Auth entirely.
   222→Future implementation can support this as fallback.
   223→```

   227→## 3. Encryption Architecture
   228→
   229→### 3.1 Encryption Primitives
   230→
   231→| Algorithm | Purpose | Standard | Implementation | Version |
   232→|-----------|---------|----------|----------------|---------|
   233→| AES-256-GCM | File content + metadata encryption | NIST | Web Crypto API | v1.0+ |
   234→| AES-256-CTR | Streaming file encryption (video/audio) | NIST | Web Crypto API | v1.1+ |
   235→| ECIES (secp256k1) | Key wrapping (asymmetric encryption of symmetric keys) | SEC 2 | ethers.js | v1.0+ |
   236→| ECDSA (secp256k1) | Signing, key derivation | NIST/SECG | Web3Auth | v1.0+ |
   237→| Ed25519 | IPNS record signing | RFC 8032 | libsodium.js | v1.0+ |
   238→| HKDF-SHA256 | Key derivation | RFC 5869 | Web Crypto API | v1.0+ |
   239→| SHA-256 | Hashing | NIST | Web Crypto API | v1.0+ |
   240→
   241→### 3.1.1 Encryption Mode Roadmap
   242→
   243→CipherBox implements a hybrid encryption approach to balance security with streaming capabilities:
   244→
   245→**v1.0 (Current): Foundation**
   246→- All files encrypted with AES-256-GCM
   247→- `encryptionMode` metadata field added to all files (set to "GCM")
   248→- Provides authenticated encryption with 16-byte authentication tag
   249→- No streaming support (full file must be downloaded before decryption)
   250→
   251→**v1.1 (Future): Hybrid GCM + CTR**
   252→- Implement AES-256-CTR encryption for streaming use cases
   253→- Auto-detect MIME type (video/audio → CTR, others → GCM)
   254→- Support chunk-by-chunk decryption for media streaming
   255→- Maintain security via IPNS signatures + IPFS CID hashing
   256→
   257→**Security Basis for CTR Mode:**
   258→
   259→While AES-256-CTR lacks per-file authentication tags, CipherBox mitigates this through:
   260→
   261→1. **IPNS Signature (Ed25519):** Every folder metadata update is signed with Ed25519, preventing CID substitution attacks
   262→2. **IPFS CID Hash:** Content-addressed storage ensures any modification to encrypted content produces a different CID
   263→3. **Metadata-Level Authentication:** The combination of IPNS signatures + CID hashing provides cryptographic integrity protection through metadata-level authentication
   264→
   265→This layered approach allows CTR streaming while maintaining zero-knowledge security guarantees.
   266→
   267→### 3.2 File Encryption (v1.0)
   268→
   269→Each file is encrypted with a unique random key:
   270→
   271→```
   272→1. Generate random fileKey (256-bit AES key)
   273→2. Generate random IV (96-bit for GCM)
   274→3. Encrypt file content:
   275→   ciphertext = AES-256-GCM(plaintext, fileKey, IV)
   276→   Output: ciphertext + 16-byte authentication tag
   277→
   278→4. Wrap fileKey with user's public key:
   279→   encryptedFileKey = ECIES(fileKey, publicKey)
   280→   Output: ephemeral_pubkey || nonce || ciphertext || auth_tag
   281→
   282→5. Store in folder metadata:
   283→   - cid: IPFS content identifier
   284→   - fileKeyEncrypted: wrapped key
   285→   - fileIv: IV for decryption
   286→   - encryptionMode: "GCM" (for all files in v1.0)
   287→```
   288→
   289→**v1.1 Roadmap Note:** Future versions will support AES-256-CTR for streaming video/audio files. The `encryptionMode` field enables this without requiring data migration. See Section 3.1.1 for security details.
   290→
   291→### 3.3 Folder Metadata Encryption
   292→
   293→Folder metadata (child list) is encrypted with the folder's key:
   294→
   295→```
   296→1. Serialize metadata to JSON
   297→2. Generate random IV (96-bit)
   298→3. Encrypt:
   299→   encryptedMetadata = AES-256-GCM(metadataJson, folderKey, IV)
   300→
   301→4. Store in IPNS record:
   302→   {
   303→     "version": "1.0",
   304→     "encryptedMetadata": "0x...",
   305→     "iv": "0x...",
   306→     "signature": "..." // IPNS signature
   307→   }
   308→```
   309→
   310→### 3.4 Decrypted Metadata Structure
   311→
   312→```json
   313→{
   314→  "children": [
   315→    {
   316→      "type": "folder",
   317→      "nameEncrypted": "0x...",
   318→      "nameIv": "0x...",
   319→      "ipnsName": "k51qzi5uqu5dlvj66...",
   320→      "ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted": "0x...",
   321→      "folderKeyEncrypted": "0x...",
   322→      "created": 1705268100,
   323→      "modified": 1705268100
   324→    },
   325→    {
   326→      "type": "file",
   327→      "nameEncrypted": "0x...",
   328→      "nameIv": "0x...",
   329→      "cid": "QmXxxx...",
   330→      "fileKeyEncrypted": "0x...",
   331→      "fileIv": "0x...",
   332→      "encryptionMode": "GCM",
   333→      "size": 2048576,
   334→      "created": 1705268100,
   335→      "modified": 1705268100
   336→    }
   337→  ],
   338→  "metadata": {
   339→    "created": 1705268100,
   340→    "modified": 1705268100
   341→  }
   342→}
   343→```
   344→
   345→**Field Descriptions:**
   346→- `encryptionMode`: Specifies the encryption algorithm used for file content ("GCM" or "CTR"). Always "GCM" in v1.0. Added to support future streaming capabilities (v1.1+). Client-side decryption logic must default to "GCM" if field is missing for backward compatibility.
   347→
   348→### 3.5 No File Deduplication
   349→
   350→CipherBox does NOT deduplicate files. Each upload uses:
   351→- Unique random 256-bit AES key
   352→- Unique random 96-bit IV
   353→
   354→Same file uploaded twice produces different ciphertexts and different CIDs. This is a security feature—deduplication would leak information about file contents.
   355→
   356→**Note:** This no-deduplication policy applies to all encryption modes (both GCM and future CTR). Each file receives unique encryption parameters regardless of the algorithm used.

   360→## 4. Key Management
   361→
   362→### 4.1 Key Hierarchy
   363→
   364→```
   365→User Authentication (Web3Auth)
   366→    │
   367→    ▼
   368→ECDSA Keypair (secp256k1)
   369→    │
   370→    ├─► privateKey
   371→    │   • Client RAM only
   372→    │   • Never transmitted
   373→    │   • Never persisted
   374→    │   • Used for: ECIES decrypt, SIWE sign
   375→    │   • Destroyed on logout
   376→    │
   377→    └─► publicKey
   378→        • Stored on CipherBox server
   379→        • Used to identify user
   380→        • Used to encrypt all data keys
   381→
   382→Root Folder Key (AES-256)
   383→    │
   384→    ├─► Generated on vault init
   385→    ├─► Stored encrypted on server: ECIES(rootFolderKey, publicKey)
   386→    └─► Decrypted client-side on login
   387→
   388→Root IPNS Private Key (Ed25519)
   389→    │
   390→    ├─► Generated on vault init
   391→    ├─► Stored encrypted on server: ECIES(ipnsPrivateKey, publicKey)
   392→    └─► Decrypted client-side for IPNS publishing
   393→
   394→Subfolder Keys (AES-256, one per folder)
   395→    │
   396→    ├─► Generated on folder creation
   397→    ├─► Stored encrypted in parent metadata
   398→    └─► Decrypted when traversing tree
   399→
   400→File Keys (AES-256, one per file)
   401→    │
   402→    ├─► Generated on file upload
   403→    ├─► Stored encrypted in folder metadata
   404→    └─► Decrypted when downloading
   405→```
   406→
   407→### 4.2 Key Storage Summary
   408→
   409→| Key | Storage Location | Encrypted With | When Decrypted |
   410→|-----|------------------|----------------|----------------|
   411→| privateKey | Client RAM only | N/A | Session lifetime |
   412→| publicKey | Server (Users table) | N/A (public) | N/A |
   413→| rootFolderKey | Server (Vaults table) | ECIES(publicKey) | On login |
   414→| rootIpnsPrivateKey | Server (Vaults table) | ECIES(publicKey) | On login |
   415→| folderKey | Parent IPNS record | ECIES(publicKey) | On folder access |
   416→| fileKey | Folder IPNS record | ECIES(publicKey) | On file download |
   417→| ipnsPrivateKey (subfolder) | Parent IPNS record | ECIES(publicKey) | On folder write |
   418→| teePublicKey (current) | Server (tee_key_state) | N/A (public) | Returned at login |
   419→| teePublicKey (previous) | Server (tee_key_state) | N/A (public) | Returned at login (grace period) |
   420→| encryptedIpnsPrivateKey (for TEE) | Server (ipns_republish_schedule) | ECIES(teePublicKey) | By TEE during republish |
   421→
   422→### 4.3 TEE Key Epochs
   423→
   424→TEE public keys are organized by epochs for key rotation:
   425→
   426→```
   427→TEE Key State (in PostgreSQL):
   428→├─► currentEpoch: 5
   429→├─► currentPublicKey: 0x04abc123...  (secp256k1)
   430→├─► previousEpoch: 4
   431→└─► previousPublicKey: 0x04def456... (4-week grace period)
   432→
   433→Client Flow:
   434→1. Login response includes teeKeys: { currentEpoch, currentPublicKey, previousEpoch, previousPublicKey }
   435→2. Client encrypts ipnsPrivateKey with currentPublicKey: ECIES(ipnsPrivateKey, teePublicKey)
   436→3. Client sends encryptedIpnsPrivateKey + keyEpoch with IPNS publish requests
   437→4. Backend stores in ipns_republish_schedule for TEE republishing
   438→```
   439→
   440→**Key Rotation (4-Week Grace Period):**
   441→- Week 0: Rotation announced (TEE governance)
   442→- Week 4: Backend detects new epoch, updates tee_key_state
   443→- Week 5: TEE republishes auto-upgrade old entries to new epoch
   444→- Week 6: Clients get new keys on login
   445→- Week 8: Old epoch deprecated
   446→
   447→### 4.4 Key Lifecycle
   448→
   449→**Session Start:**
   450→1. User authenticates via Web3Auth
   451→2. privateKey reconstructed in client RAM
   452→3. Client fetches encrypted rootFolderKey from server
   453→4. Client decrypts rootFolderKey with privateKey
   454→5. Session active
   455→
   456→**Session End:**
   457→1. User clicks logout (or session expires)
   458→2. Clear privateKey from memory
   459→3. Clear rootFolderKey from memory
   460→4. Clear all cached folder keys
   461→5. Clear all tokens
   462→
   463→### 4.5 PoC Local Key Bootstrap (Console Harness)
   464→
   465→The console PoC bypasses Web3Auth and the backend. It uses a locally provided `privateKey` and persists only the minimum vault state to disk for the duration of the run.
   466→
   467→**PoC bootstrap rules:**
   468→- Load `privateKey` from `.env` (client-only, never logged)
   469→- Derive `publicKey` locally (secp256k1)
   470→- Generate `rootFolderKey` and store on disk for the run
   471→- Generate per-folder IPNS keys on the local IPFS node
   472→- Store the IPNS key **name** encrypted with ECIES in folder metadata (stand-in for `ipnsPrivateKey`), while the actual IPNS private key remains in the local IPFS keystore
   473→
   474→**Teardown:**
   475→- Unpin all file and folder metadata CIDs created during the run
   476→- Remove any IPNS keys created in the local IPFS keystore

   480→## 5. IPFS & IPNS Architecture
   481→
   482→### 5.1 Per-Folder IPNS Records
   483→
   484→Each folder has its own IPNS record with dedicated keypair:
   485→
   486→```
   487→Root Folder
   488→├─► IPNS Name: k51qzi5uqu5dlvj55...
   489→├─► IPNS Private Key: stored encrypted on server
   490→└─► Contains: encrypted list of children
   491→
   492→Subfolder (Documents)
   493→├─► IPNS Name: k51qzi5uqu5dlvj66...
   494→├─► IPNS Private Key: stored encrypted in parent metadata
   495→└─► Contains: encrypted list of children
   496→```
   497→
   498→This design enables future per-folder sharing (v2+).
   499→
   500→### 5.2 IPNS Publishing Flow
   501→
   502→```mermaid
   503→sequenceDiagram
   504→    participant C as Client
   505→    participant B as CipherBox Backend
   506→    participant IPFS as IPFS Network
   507→    
   508→    C->>C: Update folder metadata (add/remove child)
   509→    C->>C: Encrypt metadata: AES-GCM(metadata, folderKey)
   510→    C->>C: Decrypt folder's ipnsPrivateKey
   511→  C->>B: POST /ipfs/add (encrypted metadata)
   512→  B->>IPFS: Add metadata, return CID
   513→  B->>C: Return CID
   514→  C->>C: Sign IPNS record (Ed25519)
   515→  C->>C: Encode signed record to BASE64
   516→  C->>B: POST /ipns/publish (BASE64-encoded signed record)
   517→  B->>IPFS: Publish IPNS record
   518→    Note over IPFS: IPNS name now resolves to new CID
   519→```
   520→
   521→**Key Point:** Client signs IPNS records locally; backend relays signed records only. Private keys never leave client.
   522→
   523→### 5.3 Tree Traversal
   524→
   525→```typescript
   526→async function fetchFileTree(ipnsName: string, folderKey: Uint8Array): Promise<FolderNode> {
   527→  // 1. Resolve IPNS via backend relay
   528→  const { cid } = await api.get(`/ipns/resolve?ipnsName=${ipnsName}`);
   529→  
   530→  // 2. Fetch encrypted metadata from IPFS
   531→  const encryptedData = await api.get(`/ipfs/cat?cid=${cid}`, { responseType: "arraybuffer" });
   532→  const { encryptedMetadata, iv } = JSON.parse(encryptedData);
   533→  
   534→  // 3. Decrypt metadata
   535→  const metadataJson = AES256GCM_Decrypt(encryptedMetadata, folderKey, iv);
   536→  const metadata = JSON.parse(metadataJson);
   537→  
   538→  // 4. Process children
   539→  const tree = { children: [] };
   540→  for (const child of metadata.children) {
   541→    if (child.type === "folder") {
   542→      // Decrypt subfolder key
   543→      const subfolderKey = ECIES_Decrypt(child.folderKeyEncrypted, privateKey);
   544→      // Recursively fetch subfolder
   545→      const childTree = await fetchFileTree(child.ipnsName, subfolderKey);
   546→      tree.children.push({ type: "folder", name: decrypt(child.nameEncrypted), subtree: childTree });
   547→    } else {
   548→      tree.children.push({ type: "file", name: decrypt(child.nameEncrypted), cid: child.cid });
   549→    }
   550→  }
   551→  return tree;
   552→}
   553→```
   554→
   555→### 5.4 Sync via IPNS Polling
   556→
   557→```mermaid
   558→sequenceDiagram
   559→    participant D1 as Device 1
   560→    participant B as CipherBox Backend
   561→    participant IPFS as IPFS Network
   562→    participant D2 as Device 2
   563→    
   564→    D1->>B: POST /ipfs/add + POST /ipns/publish
   565→    B->>IPFS: Relay publish
   566→    loop Every 30s
   567→    D2->>B: GET /ipns/resolve
   568→    B->>IPFS: Resolve IPNS name
   569→    B->>D2: Return current CID
   570→        D2->>D2: Compare with cached CID
   571→        alt CID changed
   572→      D2->>B: GET /ipfs/cat
   573→            D2->>D2: Decrypt and update UI
   574→        end
   575→    end
   576→```
   577→
   578→### 5.5 Conflict Resolution (v1)
   579→
   580→For v1, IPFS network determines which IPNS update wins:
   581→- IPNS records have sequence numbers
   582→- Latest valid record (highest sequence) wins
   583→- No application-level conflict resolution
   584→
   585→Future versions may implement vector clocks or CRDTs.

   589→## 6. Tech Stack
   590→
   591→| Component | Technology | Rationale |
   592→|-----------|------------|-----------|
   593→| Frontend | React 18 + TypeScript | Modern, good for encryption UI |
   594→| Web Crypto | Web Crypto API | Native browser encryption |

   605→
   606→## 7. Threat Model
   607→
   608→### 7.1 Server Compromise
   609→
   610→**Scenario:** Attacker gains access to CipherBox database and code.
   611→
   612→**What attacker has:**
   613→- Encrypted root folder keys
   614→- User public keys
   615→- Refresh token hashes
   616→- IPNS names
   617→
   618→**What attacker cannot do:**
   619→- Decrypt any files (no private keys)
   620→- Impersonate users (refresh tokens are hashed)
   621→- Access vault contents (all encrypted)
   622→
   623→**Mitigation:** Private keys never stored on server. Zero-knowledge architecture.
   624→
   625→### 7.2 Web3Auth Compromise
   626→
   627→**Scenario:** Attacker compromises Web3Auth infrastructure.
   628→
   629→**Impact:** Could potentially derive user keypairs (requires compromising threshold of nodes).
   630→
   631→**Mitigation:**
   632→- Web3Auth uses threshold cryptography (no single point of failure)
   633→- Users can export keys for independent recovery
   634→- SIWE auth validates identity without relying on Web3Auth tokens
   635→
   636→### 7.3 Network Interception
   637→
   638→**Scenario:** Attacker intercepts HTTPS traffic.
   639→
   640→**What attacker sees:**
   641→- Ciphertexts (encrypted files)
   642→- IPFS CIDs
   643→- Public keys
   644→
   645→**What attacker cannot do:**
   646→- Decrypt ciphertexts (no private keys)
   647→- Derive private key from public key
   648→
   649→**Mitigation:** HTTPS enforced, all sensitive data encrypted.
   650→
   651→### 7.4 Client Compromise
   652→
   653→**Scenario:** Attacker gains control of user's device during active session.
   654→
   655→**Impact:** Attacker can access private key in RAM.
   656→
   657→**Mitigation:**
   658→- Keys discarded on logout
   659→- Short access token expiry (15 min)
   660→- External wallet auth requires wallet approval
   661→
   662→### 7.5 Refresh Token Theft
   663→
   664→**Scenario:** Attacker steals refresh token.
   665→
   666→**Impact:** Attacker can obtain new access tokens, impersonate user.
   667→
   668→**Mitigation:**
   669→- Refresh token rotation (new token on each use)
   670→- Secure storage (HTTP-only cookie)
   671→- Short access token expiry limits exposure
   672→
   673→### 7.6 TEE Compromise
   674→
   675→**Scenario:** Attacker compromises TEE hardware or TEE provider infrastructure.
   676→
   677→**What attacker could access:**
   678→- IPNS private keys during the brief decryption window (milliseconds)
   679→- Ability to sign IPNS records for affected users
   680→
   681→**What attacker cannot do:**
   682→- Decrypt file contents (IPNS keys only sign metadata pointers, not file encryption keys)
   683→- Access vault encryption keys (stored encrypted with user's publicKey, not TEE)
   684→- Persist IPNS private keys (TEE zeroes memory after signing)
   685→- Affect users who haven't published since last TEE key rotation
   686→
   687→**Impact severity:** Medium
   688→- Attacker could point IPNS names to malicious CIDs
   689→- Users would see corrupted/fake metadata (detectable by decryption failure)
   690→- Cannot access actual file contents
   691→
   692→**Mitigation:**
   693→- TEE hardware attestation (Intel SGX/AMD SEV) verified before key operations
   694→- IPNS private keys decrypted only for milliseconds, then zeroed
   695→- 4-week key epoch rotation limits exposure window
   696→- Multi-epoch fallback allows rapid migration to new TEE keys
   697→- Primary provider (Phala Cloud) with fallback (AWS Nitro) for provider diversification
   698→- Monitoring: republish success rate, epoch lag, unusual patterns
   699→
